session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Participants will be framed as men reflecting on their own everyday lives — the specific places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep. The collective identity is 'men in the UK thinking about how they live day-to-day', not researchers or experts on masculinity. I will avoid framing them as people with opinions on gender theory and instead keep the anchor concrete: what they actually do, eat, and experience.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or defensively dismissive answers ('gender doesn't affect what I eat'). Will require behavioural grounding early — getting to specific moments and past events rather than general attitudes.

Social acceptability of plant-based foods (Sections 4–5): Risk of consensus hardening quickly around practical/cost barriers, masking deeper identity and social concerns. Will need sharpening moves and dissent invitations.

The relationship between masculine identity and food: Participants may hold implicit associations between meat and masculinity without being able to name them directly. Contradictions between stated positions and described behaviours are the most valuable data here — must track carefully.

What would actually need to change for plant-based eating to be viable (Section 4): Risk of abstract or aspirational answers. Need to keep this grounded in real constraints — social, practical, emotional — not just stated preferences.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Unknown from profile alone — 45, suburban South East. May be relatively comfortable in group settings given age and context, but no strong prior anticipation.

48, suburban East of England. Oldest of the group by a small margin. May be more settled in his views; could either anchor the group or resist novelty. Worth watching for early opinion-leadership signals.

45, suburban South West. No distinguishing profile markers. Monitor for early reticence — South West context sometimes associated with more traditional attitudes that could feel less speakable in a group.

40, suburban North West. Youngest of the group by 5 years. May hold somewhat different reference points from the others. Worth tracking whether he self-positions as different from the older participants.

known_risk_conditions: Topic produces socially desirable answers by design — men discussing gender and food choices are likely to present themselves as more flexible or enlightened than their actual behaviour. Behavioural grounding (specific past events, real meals, named occasions) is essential from Section 2 onward.

Consensus risk is structurally high in an all-male group on a topic that touches masculine identity — participants may align around a shared 'laddish pragmatism' frame that masks real diversity. Must watch for premature convergence, especially in Sections 3–5.

The word 'gender' (Section 3 scripted question) may trigger a defensive or intellectualised response. If participants pivot to abstract gender-theory language or blanket dismissal ('no, I just eat what I fancy'), will need a quick behavioural redirect without leading.

Plant-based eating carries active stigma in some male social contexts — participants may perform indifference or mild hostility for social reasons rather than expressing genuine attitudes. Indirect probing (social context, what others think, specific scenarios) will be more useful than direct attitude questions.
Group is entirely suburban UK men in their 40s — high homogeneity increases conformity risk. Need to work harder to surface genuine diversity of experience than with a mixed-profile group.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1 (intro, opening context): Very light touch. The goal is rapport and getting voices in the room. Minimal probing — enough to hear from everyone, not enough to exhaust the warmup topics. Section 2 (everyday food decisions): Moderate directivity. Begin transitioning from general attitudes to specific behaviours. Introduce behavioural grounding here so the norm is established before we hit the sensitive sections. Sections 3–5 (main topics): Highest directivity. Active use of contradictions, dissent invitations, and behavioural probes. Do not let abstract answers stand unchallenged. Use sharpening moves when consensus forms too quickly. Section 6 (closing): Very light. Offer space for addition but do not reopen closed topics or probe for depth.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the core research weight and receive the largest share combined (~55% of total budget). Context sections (1, 2) serve as warm-up and behavioural grounding and receive a moderate share (~30%). Intro and closing are functional bookends and receive minimal budget (~15% combined).

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
discussion_guide.section_purpose: Section 1: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

suggested_probes: Do other people influence what you eat? If so, tell us more about how.
Do your work or hobbies influence what foods you eat? Tell us more about how.
How important is health and nutrition?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about
why or why not.
suggested_probes: Is it socially acceptable for men to eat vegetarian or vegan foods?

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Imagine you decided to go plant-based — what would need to change in
your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?
How might it change the way you shop or cook?

unresolved_tensions.description: opened by saying 'we made a conscious choice' to share food responsibilities, but then said 'I'm not sure I would've ended up doing the planning and the cooking together thing if she hadn't... suggested it' — the choice was less mutual than the initial framing implied

group_has_agreed_easily_on: Mental vs physical fatigue leads to different ways of unwinding — desk workers want to get out and be social, physical workers want something quieter and hands-on.

last_engagement_round.hook: Nick's point about it not being just his choice hits something — the plant-based thing would affect his wife and kid, but there's also something about what he's saying that feels like it needs pushing on a bit. He's framing it all as 'not feasible' and 'would need everyone on board' but there's a difference between that and just... not wanting to do it himself. I've been talking about self-respect and looking after yourself — but Nick's situation is the opposite problem. He's so focused on what works for everyone else that I'm not sure he's actually considering what he wants, or whether he's just defaulting to 'it's complicated so we won't.' That's different from Paul's situation where they actually had the conversation and made a joint decision. Nick sounds like he hasn't even asked the question for himself yet.

Nick's just said something important about family decisions not being individual choices, and about the practical impossibility of making big dietary shifts without everyone on board. That's hitting close to home for me — not kids, but it's made me realize I've been defensive about my own setup when actually Nick's naming something real about constraints and compromise that I haven't properly acknowledged.

Nick's point about not being able to decide alone in a family situation is hitting me — I'm solo, so I've had the opposite problem. The plant-based question made me realize something about my own choices that I haven't said yet.

Paul's point about needing a conscious conversation to shift the default gender dynamics — that resonates with my own experience, and I think there's something about how that conversation happens (or doesn't) when you're time-poor that hasn't been touched on yet

Nick's point about needing family agreement on something like plant-based eating connects directly to what I said about gender and conversations—it's the same pattern. Big decisions don't just happen, they need actual discussion. And there's something about the reality check he's giving that I recognize from my own experience—the difference between what sounds good in theory and what actually works when you're managing real constraints.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was purely introductory — participants established geographic and occupational identity (construction, electrical, HR, work-from-home) and briefly signalled life-stage differences around family and commuting. A spontaneous theme of work-life balance emerged organically across several introductions, with participants triangulating their own situations against each other's. No substantive topic has yet been explored; the section functioned as social orientation rather than thematic discussion.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator kept the opening brief and low-stakes, using a round-robin geography prompt to get everyone speaking early. The spontaneous balance thread that emerged was noted but sensibly not pursued — the moderator redirected cleanly into the first substantive question. Allowing participants to self-introduce without interruption worked well; all four spoke voluntarily and unprompted, suggesting a comfortable early group dynamic.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on leisure time and socialising, with life-stage and work-type emerging as the dominant structuring forces. A productive contrast developed between physical and mental fatigue as drivers of different unwinding styles, while a deeper tension surfaced around freedom versus constraint — those without domestic responsibilities describing expansive, self-directed time, and those with young families or home-working arrangements describing compressed, fitted-in socialising. Notably, Nick reframed constraint as focus rather than deprivation, complicating a simple freedom/restriction binary.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The moderator largely let Andrew and John's organic exchange run, intervening only when it risked excluding the remaining three. Direct address to Paul successfully retrieved a quiet voice. The section transition felt clean and timely — the life-stage theme had reached a natural resolution in Nick and Paul's contributions. Allowing participant-to-participant dialogue to develop the mental/physical fatigue distinction worked well; the moderator's light touch preserved authenticity without losing direction.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: Food organised this section, but the real terrain was self-concept and constraint. A productive early contrast between fuel and ritual (Daniel vs Paul) resolved quickly into mutual respect, then the section deepened unexpectedly: Andrew reframed solo eating around self-respect rather than accountability, prompting John to revise his own position in real time. The life-stage/circumstance theme from earlier carried forward, but was complicated by the suggestion that intentionality is a choice independent of domestic structure.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening redirect to Andrew, John, and Nick after Daniel and Paul's exchange was well-timed — it retrieved three voices and introduced the solo-living dimension, which proved generative. Allowing Andrew and John's exchange to run without intervention was the right call; John's live position-shift was the section's most candid moment. Nick was held for last as a transition device, which risks his contribution feeling rushed — that's a marginal concern worth watching into the next section.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section closed the food discussion with Nick's contribution, which reframed the constraint/choice tension from earlier: domestic responsibility as a structural enforcer of standards rather than a burden or a virtue. The self-respect thread from the previous section carried forward but was complicated — for Nick, consistency isn't chosen, it's imposed. The section then pivoted sharply into new territory with the gender-influence question, leaving that theme entirely unresolved.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Nick had been held back as a transition device and delivered a useful bridging contribution — the concern about him feeling rushed appears unfounded. The gender question was introduced cleanly, framed to pre-empt social desirability bias by distinguishing practice from prescription. It's a significant pivot; the risk is it arrives before Nick's thread was fully exhausted. Whether that abruptness costs anything depends on how the group engages the new question.

transcript.content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Sarah, and I'll be facilitating the conversation. There genuinely are no right or wrong answers here — we're interested in what you actually think and do, not what sounds like the correct thing to say. It's a conversation, not an interview, so if something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in — you don't need to wait to be asked. I work in electrical and electronics, so I'm out on the road most days installing stuff, travelling between different sites. Got a wife, a young kid at home, and yeah — trying to keep all that balanced really. That's me.

I'm Paul, South East, suburban like you Nick. Yeah, I get what you mean about the balance thing. I work from home though, so it's a bit different — no commute, which helps. But I'm in HR and training, supporting people through recruitment and that sort of stuff. So it's still juggling work and home, just without the travel element you've got. My wife and I, no kids at home, so I suppose we've got it a bit easier than you in that respect. But yeah, South East suburban crew here as well.

Yeah, I'm Daniel, East of England — suburban area like you lot. And I hear what you're saying, Nick. I'm in construction, building finishing work mostly, so I'm out on sites all over the region pretty much every day. Not quite as far afield as you might be, but still driving around, different locations all the time. 

The balance thing — yeah, that resonates. My wife's working too, so it's not like one of us is holding the fort at home. We've got the house sorted, no kids living with us anymore, which I suppose makes it easier than what Nick's dealing with. But it's still that juggling act of early starts, getting back in the evening, trying to keep on top of things at home. Different from Paul's setup where he's at least there during the day.

Great, thanks everyone — good to know who's in the room. So we've got construction, electrical, HR, and a mix of family setups across the South East, South West, North West, and East of England. Right, let's get into it. First question — and feel free to be as specific as you like here — what's your favourite place in your city or town to spend time with your male friends? Could be a pub, a sports ground, someone's garage, anywhere really. What do you lot actually do?

One's just walking distance from where I live, so that's handy on a Friday or Saturday evening. Nothing fancy, just a decent local where you can actually hear people talk, you know? Not one of those places where the music's so loud you're basically lip-reading your mates.

I'll head out that way when I can, bit of a drive, clear your head. Nothing organised really, just grab the van sometimes and head out, maybe stop somewhere different. You're right about the pub thing too though — there's a couple of decent locals I'll go to, but honestly with the hours I'm doing most weeks I'm knackered by the time the weekend comes. So a lot of it ends up being work on the van, bit of tinkering in the driveway, and then yeah, if the weather's decent or I've got the energy, get out for a drive. But the pub's not really a regular thing for me, not like it sounds like it is for you. Just depends how I'm feeling really.
